claim: Urea constitutes about half of the nitrogen applied to crop production globally and is the most widely used nitrogen fertilizer in agriculture.
source: Urea, a key synthetic nitrogen source, constitutes about half of the nitrogen applied to crop production globally and is the most widely used nitrogen fertilizer in agriculture (http://faostat.fao.org).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to FAO statistics (http://faostat.fao.org).

claim: Arginase is the only enzyme in plants known to generate urea in vivo.
source: Arginase (ARGAH; arginine amidinohydrolase), the only enzyme in plants known to generate urea in vivo, plays a pivotal role in the mobilization of seed storage reserves during early seedling growth post-germination.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact about plant biochemistry.

claim: Arginine has the highest nitrogen-to-carbon ratio (N:C = 4:6) among all amino acids.
source: Arginine, abundant in the storage proteins of most plant seeds, has the highest nitrogen-to-carbon ratio (N:C = 4:6) among all amino acids, making it a significant nitrogen source for seed reserve mobilization (Jones and Boulter, 1968; King and Gifford, 1997; Polacco et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: In a study of 379 angiosperm seeds, arginine accounted for 17% of the seed nitrogen content.
source: In a study of 379 angiosperm seeds, arginine accounted for 17% of the seed nitrogen content (8.58 g arginine/16 g seed N) (Van Etten et al., 1967).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Van Etten et al., 1967.

claim: Arginine serves as a substrate for nitric oxide (NO) and polyamine (PA) biosynthesis in plants by nitric oxide synthase (NOS) and arginine decarboxylase (ADC).
source: Beyond its hydrolysis by arginase to yield urea, arginine also serves as a substrate for nitric oxide (NO) and polyamine (PA) biosynthesis in plants by nitric oxide synthase (NOS) and arginine decarboxylase (ADC) (Siddappa and Marathe, 2020), respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Siddappa and Marathe, 2020.

claim: Arginine is a shared substrate, competitively utilized by the three enzymes ARGAH, NOS, and ADC.
source: Consequently, arginine becomes a shared substrate, competitively utilized by the three enzymes ARGAH, NOS, and ADC (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1 which illustrates the competitive enzymatic interactions.

claim: The addition of 5 μM NOHA into NaCl medium significantly increased the germination rate of wild-type Arabidopsis seeds under salt stress.
source: However, the addition of 5 μM NOHA into NaCl medium significantly increased the germination rate (Figure 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The inhibitory effect of salt on seed germination was significantly alleviated by increasing NOHA concentrations.
source: The results showed that the inhibitory effect of salt on seed germination was significantly alleviated by the increasing NOHA concentrations, while NOHA added in control medium had no substantial effect (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: NOHA could promote root growth under salt stress conditions.
source: Additionally, root length measurements taken 14 days after germination indicated that NOHA could promote root growth under salt stress conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The addition of 15 µM of PPD increased the germination rate to 70% under salt stress, compared with less than 10% without PPD.
source: The results showed that salt significantly inhibited the germination of wild-type Arabidopsis seeds, with less than 10% germination. The addition of 15 µM of PPD increased the germination rate to 70%, compared with the rate without PPD (Figure 1d), which showed the same trend as NOHA treatment (Figure 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Urea hydrolysis may be the leading cause of salt-induced inhibition of seed germination (SISG).
source: These results indicate that salt tolerance in WT seeds germination and seedling growth is manifested especially under NOHA and PPD conditions. The two-step hydrolysis pathway of arginine mediated by arginase and its downstream metabolite urea hydrolase is not only involved in SISG events, but also urea hydrolysis may be the leading cause of SISG occurrence.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results with NOHA and PPD treatments.

claim: Arabidopsis thaliana has two genes encoding ARGAH, namely ARGAH1 (gene number: AT4G08900) and ARGAH2 (gene number: AT4G08870).
source: Arabidopsis thaliana has two genes encoding ARGAH, namely ARGAH1 (gene number: AT4G08900) and ARGAH2 (gene number: AT4G08870).
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the Arabidopsis genome.

claim: AtArgAH1 has a T-DNA insertion within its first exon, while AtArgAH2 contains a T-DNA insertion in the fourth exon.
source: AtArgAH1 has a T-DNA insertion within its first exon, while AtArgAH2 contains a T-DNA insertion in the fourth exon. Consequently, the mutants resulting from these insertions were denoted as argah1 and argah2, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1a showing the T-DNA insertion sites.

claim: The seed germination rates of each mutant (argah1, argah2, and argah1/argah2) were significantly higher than those of WT under NaCl conditions.
source: The seed germination rates of each mutant (argah1, argah2, and argah1/argah2) were significantly higher than those of WT under NaCl conditions (Figure 2c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The root length of the mutant under salt stress was significantly higher than that of the WT.
source: Furthermore, the root length of the mutant under salt stress was significantly higher than that of the WT (Figure 2d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Arginase activity analysis revealed significantly lower levels in argah1, argah2, and argah1/argah2 mutants following NaCl treatment compared to WT.
source: Moreover, arginase activity analysis revealed significantly lower levels in argah1, argah2, and argah1/argah2 mutants following NaCl treatment compared to WT (Figure 2e).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Partial or complete blocking of the arginine hydrolysis pathway can effectively alleviate SISG.
source: These findings indicate that partial or complete blocking of the arginine hydrolysis pathway can effectively alleviate SISG.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the mutant analysis results.

claim: The accumulation of urea in vivo, derived from the hydrolysis of arginine by arginase, is insufficient to trigger SISG.
source: We have previously reported that deletion mutants of the urea hydrolase gene (urease) enhance salt tolerance during seed germination (Bu et al., 2015). That implies that even the accumulation of urea in vivo, derived from the hydrolysis of arginine by arginase, is insufficient to trigger SISG.
evidence: The claim is inferred from previous research cited (Bu et al., 2015).

claim: SOS3 binds to free Ca2+, consequently activating SOS2 protein kinase, which in turn phosphorylates SOS1, leading to the activation of SOS1 transport responsible for pumping Na+ out of the cell.
source: It is well known that Na+ toxicity is the main factor triggering SISG. The mechanism involves SOS3 binds to free Ca2+, consequently activating SOS2 protein kinase, which in turn phosphorylates SOS1, leading to the activation of SOS1 transport responsible for pumping Na+ out of the cell (Zhou et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhou et al., 2022.

claim: SOS3-deficient mutant (sos3) accumulate substantial Na+ levels and are highly sensitive to salt stress.
source: Therefore, SOS3-deficient mutant (sos3) accumulate substantial Na+ levels and are highly sensitive to salt stress.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact about the sos3 mutant.

claim: With increasing concentrations of PPD, the growth inhibition of sos3 induced by NaCl was alleviated significantly.
source: Notably, with increasing the concentrations of PPD, the growth inhibition of sos3 induced by NaCl was alleviated significantly (Figure 3a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Both seed germination rate and 14-day root length of sos3 were significantly increased with PPD treatment compared to those without PPD treatment.
source: Furthermore, both seed germination rate (Figure 3b) and 14-day root length (Figure 3c) were significantly increased compared to those without PPD treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3b and 3c.

claim: The aturease/sos3 double mutant showed a significant improvement in germination ability and growth compared to sos3 in the presence of 50 mM NaCl.
source: Subsequently, the aturease/sos3 double mutant analysis revealed a significant improvement in germination ability and growth compared to sos3 in the presence of 50 mM NaCl (Figure 3d and e).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3d and 3e.

claim: The root length of aturease/sos3 double mutant exceeded that of sos3 mutants under salt stress conditions.
source: In addition, the root length of aturease/sos3 double mutant exceeded that of sos3 mutants under salt stress conditions (Figure 3f).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3f.

claim: Blocking the hydrolysis of arginine-derived urea can mitigate the hypersensitivity of sos3 to salt stress.
source: The above treatments with urea hydrolase inhibitors PPD, coupled with genetic evidence, suggest that blocking the hydrolysis of arginine-derived urea can mitigate the hypersensitivity of sos3 to salt stress.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the PPD treatment and genetic evidence with sos3 mutants.

claim: Urea accumulation in vivo is not the primary trigger of SISG.
source: This further corroborates the fact that urea accumulation in vivo is not the primary trigger of SISG. Instead, urea hydrolysis appears to play a dominant role in this process.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results with PPD and genetic mutants.

claim: NaCl stress resulted in the accumulation of urea during WT seed germination.
source: Initially, we confirmed that NaCl stress resulted in the accumulation of urea (Figure 4a) and NH4+ (Figure 4b) during WT seed germination, suggesting that salt stress promoted seed nitrogen mobilization and significantly lowered urea and NH4+ levels in the argah1/argah2 double mutants (Figure 4a and b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: NaCl stress resulted in the accumulation of NH4+ during WT seed germination.
source: Initially, we confirmed that NaCl stress resulted in the accumulation of urea (Figure 4a) and NH4+ (Figure 4b) during WT seed germination, suggesting that salt stress promoted seed nitrogen mobilization and significantly lowered urea and NH4+ levels in the argah1/argah2 double mutants (Figure 4a and b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Salt stress promoted seed nitrogen mobilization.
source: Initially, we confirmed that NaCl stress resulted in the accumulation of urea (Figure 4a) and NH4+ (Figure 4b) during WT seed germination, suggesting that salt stress promoted seed nitrogen mobilization and significantly lowered urea and NH4+ levels in the argah1/argah2 double mutants (Figure 4a and b).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the accumulation of urea and NH4+ under salt stress.

claim: Salt stress significantly lowered urea and NH4+ levels in the argah1/argah2 double mutants.
source: Initially, we confirmed that NaCl stress resulted in the accumulation of urea (Figure 4a) and NH4+ (Figure 4b) during WT seed germination, suggesting that salt stress promoted seed nitrogen mobilization and significantly lowered urea and NH4+ levels in the argah1/argah2 double mutants (Figure 4a and b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4a and 4b.

claim: In the presence of 50 mM NaCl, sos3-mutant seeds accumulated higher NH4+ levels than WT and aturease mutants.
source: In addition, in the presence of 50 mM NaCl, sos3-mutant seeds accumulated higher NH4+ levels than WT and aturease mutants.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing NH4+ levels in different mutants.

claim: The aturease/sos3 double mutant effectively reduced NH4+ levels to those akin to WT and aturease.
source: Remarkably, the aturease/sos3 double mutant effectively reduced NH4+ levels to those akin to WT and aturease (Figure 4c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Exogenous NH4+ significantly alleviated the inhibitory effects of NaCl on seed germination.
source: Surprisingly, exogenous NH4+ significantly alleviated the inhibitory effects of NaCl on seed germination (Figure 4d, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), with a concomitant increase in NH4+ (Figure 4e), indicating that NH4+ accumulation was not the primary cause of SISG.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4d and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: NH4+ accumulation was not the primary cause of SISG.
source: Surprisingly, exogenous NH4+ significantly alleviated the inhibitory effects of NaCl on seed germination (Figure 4d, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), with a concomitant increase in NH4+ (Figure 4e), indicating that NH4+ accumulation was not the primary cause of SISG.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that exogenous NH4+ alleviated SISG despite increasing NH4+ levels.

claim: Urea substantially inhibited seed germination under salt stress.
source: Intriguingly, urea substantially inhibited seed germination (Figure 4d, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), but NH4+ content did not accumulate in seeds (Figure 4e), thereby confirming that NH4+ produced via urea hydrolysis was not the driving force behind SISG.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4d and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: NH4+ produced via urea hydrolysis was not the driving force behind SISG.
source: Intriguingly, urea substantially inhibited seed germination (Figure 4d, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), but NH4+ content did not accumulate in seeds (Figure 4e), thereby confirming that NH4+ produced via urea hydrolysis was not the driving force behind SISG.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that urea inhibited germination without NH4+ accumulation.

claim: MSX significantly inhibited the germination of WT seeds under salt stress.
source: To verify the relationship between acid stress of NH4+ assimilation by GS and plant salt sensitivity, we added GS inhibitor l-methionine sulfoximine (MSX) to a salt-stress medium to inhibit NH4+ assimilation (Kiyomiya et al., 2001; Rawat Suman et al., 1999) and found that MSX significantly inhibited the germination of WT seeds under salt stress, while WT germinated well in the control medium (Figure 5a and b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5a and 5b.

claim: The percentage of seedlings with green cotyledons and root growth was severely restricted under salt-stress conditions with MSX treatment.
source: In addition, the percentage of seedlings with green cotyledons (Figure 5c) and root growth (Figure 5d) was severely restricted under salt-stress conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5c and 5d.

claim: The acidification process of GS assimilation is beneficial to plant resistance to salt stress.
source: These results suggest that the acidification process of GS assimilation is beneficial to plant resistance to salt stress.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the MSX inhibition experiments.

claim: NaCl-treated seeds showed a trend toward alkalinization compared to the control, especially evident in the epidermal cells of the root elongation zone.
source: Then, we qualitatively observed panoramic pH in germinating seeds revealing a trend toward alkalinization in NaCl-treated seeds compared to the control (no salt treatment), especially evident in the epidermal cells of the root elongation zone (Figure 6b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6b using PRpHluorin fluorescence.

claim: The addition of PPD effectively alleviated the alkalinization of the cells under salt treatment conditions, restoring their pH to levels similar to the control.
source: However, the addition of PPD effectively alleviated this alkalinization of the cells under salt treatment conditions, restoring their pH to levels similar to the control.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from pH measurements.

claim: The average cytoplasmic pH of the control was 7.07, and this pH significantly increased by 0.76 units after salt treatment.
source: The results showed that the average cytoplasmic pH of the control was 7.07, and this pH significantly increased by 0.76 units after salt treatment (Student's t-test, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative pH measurements with statistical analysis.

claim: Salt treatment with PPD restored the pH similar to the level observed in the control.
source: In contrast, salt treatment with PPD restored the pH similar to the level observed in the control (Figure 6b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Exogenous salt plus urea treatment led to a clear trend toward higher pH in root cells compared to the salt-only treatment.
source: Additionally, exogenous salt plus urea treatment led to a clear trend toward higher pH in root cells compared to the salt-only treatment (Figure 6b and c), further affirming that the increase in intracellular pH induced by urea hydrolysis inhibited seed germination.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6b and 6c.

claim: Excessive hydrolysis of arginine-derived urea elevates the cytoplasmic pH of seed radical cells, triggering SISG and impeding seedling growth in Arabidopsis thaliana.
source: Excessive hydrolysis of arginine-derived urea elevates the cytoplasmic pH of seed radical cells, triggering SISG and impeding seedling growth in Arabidopsis thaliana.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the pH measurement experiments and their correlation with germination outcomes.

claim: Under nonstressed normal conditions (control), root urea concentrations were lower in atdur3 plants than in WT plants.
source: Under nonstressed normal conditions (control), root urea concentrations were lower in atdur3 plants than in WT plants, but urea levels in cotyledons had no significant difference (Figure 7d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7d.

claim: When plants were grown under NaCl stress, the urea levels were lower in atdur3 roots than in WT roots, but urea levels were higher in atdur3 cotyledons than in WT cotyledons.
source: However, when plants were grown under NaCl stress, the urea levels were lower in atdur3 roots than in WT roots. Still, urea levels were higher in atdur3 cotyledons than in WT cotyledons (Figure 7d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7d.

claim: Urea was mainly accumulated in atdur3 cotyledons under control or NaCl conditions.
source: We further analyzed the change ratio of urea (cotyledon/root), and the results show that urea was mainly accumulated in atdur3 cotyledons under control or NaCl conditions (Figure 7e).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7e.

claim: Blocking the transport of arginine-derived urea from the cotyledon to the root is conducive to the alleviation of SISG.
source: These results further indicate that the transport of urea, the primary metabolite of arginine hydrolysis, plays an important role in SISG, that is, blocking the transport of arginine-derived urea from the cotyledon to the root is conducive to the alleviation of SISG.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the atdur3 mutant analysis showing differential urea accumulation.

claim: The germination rate of atdur3 mutant seeds was significantly higher than that of WT under salt stress.
source: On the control medium supplemented with NaCl, the germination ability of WT seeds was significantly inhibited (the ability of radicle to break through the seed coat), and the germination rate of atdur3 mutant seeds was significantly higher than that of WT (Figure 7a and b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7a and 7b.

claim: Blocking urea transport in vivo could effectively alleviate SISG.
source: These results suggest that blocking urea transport in vivo could effectively alleviate SISG.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the atdur3 mutant germination results.

claim: Seeds of O. sativa and G. max exhibited robust germination in the control medium with or without PPD.
source: The seeds of O. sativa and G. max exhibited robust germination in the control medium with or without PPD. However, germination of seeds was notably inhibited in salt medium, a hindrance significantly improved by additional of PPD (Figure 8a and b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 8a and 8b.

claim: Germination of O. sativa and G. max seeds was notably inhibited in salt medium, a hindrance significantly improved by addition of PPD.
source: The seeds of O. sativa and G. max exhibited robust germination in the control medium with or without PPD. However, germination of seeds was notably inhibited in salt medium, a hindrance significantly improved by additional of PPD (Figure 8a and b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 8a and 8b.

claim: Without PPD, germination rate of O. sativa and G. max was 20–30% in the presence of NaCl, but with PPD supplementation, germination rates significantly increased to approximately 60–80%.
source: Without PPD, germination rate was 20–30% in the presence of NaCl, but with PPD supplementation, germination rates significantly increased to approximately 60–80% (Figure 8a and b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 8a and 8b.

claim: Root lengths of O. sativa and G. max seedlings were significantly shorter in NaCl medium compared to control conditions, yet supplementation with PPD in the NaCl medium led to increased root lengths.
source: Furthermore, root lengths of the seedlings were significantly shorter in NaCl medium compared to control conditions, yet supplementation with PPD in the NaCl medium led to increased root lengths (Figure 8c and d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 8c and 8d.

claim: Under NaCl conditions, treatment with PPD significantly reduced salt-stress-induced inhibition of shoot and root growth in halophytic plants compared to untreated counterparts.
source: Similarly, studies on the typical halophytic plants demonstrated that under NaCl conditions treatment with PPD significantly reduced salt-stress-induced inhibition of shoot and root growth compared to untreated counterparts (Figure 8e).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8e.

claim: Root lengths of halophytic plant samples treated with PPD under NaCl conditions were significantly higher than those without PPD treatment.
source: Notably, root lengths of samples treated with PPD under NaCl conditions were significantly higher than those without PPD treatment (Figure 8f).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8f.

claim: Blocking arginase-dependent arginine catabolism can enhance salt-tolerant seed germination in both crops and halophytes.
source: These observations collectively suggest that blocking arginase-dependent arginine catabolism can enhance salt-tolerant seed germination in both crops and halophytes, underscoring the universal effect of arginine catabolism on plant salt tolerance.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the PPD treatment results across multiple plant species.

claim: The loss of food due to farmland salinization is estimated to have an economic impact exceeding $27 billion annually.
source: The loss of food due to farmland salinization is staggering, with an estimated economic impact of exceeding $27 billion annually (Zörb et al., 2019; Kaleem et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zörb et al., 2019 and Kaleem et al., 2018.

claim: Salt stress not only delays germination but also reduces the overall percent of successful germination.
source: Failure of seeds to germinate stands as a significant contributor to crop loss, particularly under salt stress conditions, which not only delays germination but also reduces the overall percent of successful germination (Kojima et al., 2006; Kazachkova et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kojima et al., 2006 and Kazachkova et al., 2016.

claim: Arginase-deficient mutants exhibit increased tolerance to various abiotic stresses, including water deficit, salt, and freezing.
source: For example, ARGAH knockout mutants exhibit increased tolerance to various abiotic stresses, including water deficit, salt, and freezing, while lines overexpressing AtARGAH show decreased tolerance to these stresses (Shi et al., 2013b; Flores et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Shi et al., 2013b; Flores et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2011.

claim: Terrestrial plants might not possess animal-like NOS enzymes.
source: However, subsequent studies suggest that terrestrial plants might not possess animal-like NOS enzymes (Zhao et al., 2015; Santolini et al., 2017; Jeandroz et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zhao et al., 2015; Santolini et al., 2017; Jeandroz et al., 2016.

claim: Arabidopsis nitric oxide synthase 1 (AtNOS1) was different from NOS, leading to its renaming as AtNOA1.
source: These studies showed that Arabidopsis nitric oxide synthase 1 (AtNOS1) was different from NOS, leading to its renaming as AtNOA1.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact about AtNOS1/AtNOA1.

claim: The activity of arginase and urease is particularly heightened under salt stress conditions.
source: During seed germination, the activity of arginase and urease, especially particularly heightened under salt stress conditions, facilitates the conversion of arginine to urea and then into the ammonia pool (Polacco et al., 2013; Siddappa and Marathe, 2020; Kojima et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Polacco et al., 2013; Siddappa and Marathe, 2020; Kojima et al., 2006.

claim: Arginase activity was significantly upregulated under salt stress.
source: Notably, arginase activity was significantly upregulated under salt stress (Figure 2e; Polacco et al., 2013; Siddappa and Marathe, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2e and citations to Polacco et al., 2013; Siddappa and Marathe, 2020.

claim: Salt-induced expression of arginase and urease genes occurs during seed germination.
source: This induction is further supported by strong evidence demonstrating the salt-induced expression of arginase and urease genes during seed germination (Polacco et al., 2013; Siddappa and Marathe, 2020; Kazachkova et al., 2016; Lai et al., 2020), and triggers significant accumulation of urea and NH4+ (Figure 4a and b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Polacco et al., 2013; Siddappa and Marathe, 2020; Kazachkova et al., 2016; Lai et al., 2020.

claim: The arginine hydrolysis pathway is induced by salt stress.
source: Together, these results indicate that the arginine hydrolysis pathway is induced by salt stress.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the evidence of increased arginase/urease activity and gene expression under salt stress.

claim: Glutamine synthetase 2 (GLN2), primarily located in plastid, induces acid stress through assimilation of NH4+, which exerts toxic effects on plants.
source: Recent studies have shed light on the role of glutamine synthetase 2 (GLN2), primarily located in plastid, in inducing acid stress through assimilation of NH4+, which exerts toxic effects on plants (Hachiya et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hachiya et al., 2021.

claim: MSX treatment fails to alleviate SISG under salt stress.
source: In addition, our results showed that MSX treatment fails to alleviate SISG under salt stress, and interestingly, SISG shows a negative correlation with GS activity (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: SISG shows a negative correlation with GS activity.
source: In addition, our results showed that MSX treatment fails to alleviate SISG under salt stress, and interestingly, SISG shows a negative correlation with GS activity (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Assimilation of NH4+ by GS may serve as an adaptive strategy for SISG.
source: This indicates that assimilation of NH4+ by GS may serve as an adaptive strategy for SISG.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the MSX treatment results and the negative correlation between SISG and GS activity.

claim: The hydrolysis of urea produces hydroxide ions (OH-) in addition to NH4+ and HCO3-.
source: Traditionally, the hydrolysis of urea has been considered to produce ammonia and CO2; in fact, the urea hydrolysis in the two-step hydrolysis reaction of the arginine hydrolysis pathway, '(NH2)2CO + 3H2O → 2NH4+ + HCO3−+OH−', is indeed an alkalinization reaction.
evidence: The claim is based on the chemical equation for urea hydrolysis.

claim: Further hydrolysis of bicarbonate will also produce hydroxide, leading to further alkalization.
source: In addition, further hydrolysis of bicarbonate will also produce hydroxide 'HCO3− + H2O ⇆ H2CO3+OH−', leading to further alkalization.
evidence: The claim is based on the chemical equilibrium for bicarbonate hydrolysis.

claim: Cytosolic pH (pHcyt) acts as a pivotal regulator for numerous intracellular processes.
source: Changes in cell parameters, including cytosolic pH (pHcyt), play a crucial role in both sensory and protective processes in plants under stress conditions. pHcyt acts as a pivotal regulator for numerous intracellular processes (Felle, 2001; Gjetting et al., 2012; Shen et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Felle, 2001; Gjetting et al., 2012; Shen et al., 2013.

claim: Root tissue plays a key role in plants' sensitivity to salinity.
source: It appears that root tissue plays a key role in plants' sensitivity to salinity (Yang and Lee, 2023; Wu et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yang and Lee, 2023; Wu et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2015.

claim: Salt stress leads to an increase in intracellular pH of the radicle.
source: Our investigation revealed that salt stress leads to an increase in cytoplasmic pH of seed radical cells, which results in SISG (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Blocking arginase or urease activity under salt-stressed conditions can effectively mitigate the events leading to SISG.
source: Overall, these hypothetical models suggest that blocking arginase or urease activity under salt-stressed conditions can effectively mitigate the events leading to SISG, both depending on whether the alkaline hydrolysis reaction of the core metabolite urea occurs or is enhanced, providing new insights into SISG (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results with inhibitors and mutants.

claim: In addition to Na+ toxicity, SISG is also instigated by elevated intracellular pH resulting from urea hydrolysis.
source: Therefore, we posit that, in addition to Na+ toxicity, SISG is also instigated by elevated intracellular pH resulting from urea hydrolysis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the pH measurement results and their correlation with SISG.

claim: Salt sensitivity of sos3 can be ameliorated by blocking urease activity and reducing intracellular pH under salt stress.
source: Salt sensitivity of sos3 can be ameliorated by blocking urease activity and reducing intracellular pH under salt stress.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the sos3/aturease double mutant analysis.

claim: Urea can be transported across plant cell membranes by high- or low-affinity transporters.
source: In general, urea can be transported across plant cell membranes by high- or low-affinity transporters (Polacco et al., 2013; Kojima et al., 2006; Bohner et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Polacco et al., 2013; Kojima et al., 2006; Bohner et al., 2015.

claim: Low-affinity urea transporters are mediated by PIP/TIP or TIP aqueous proteins on cellular and mitochondrial membranes.
source: On the cellular and mitochondrial membranes, low-affinity urea transporters are mediated by PIP/TIP or TIP aqueous proteins, respectively (Kojima et al., 2006; Bohner et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kojima et al., 2006; Bohner et al., 2015.

claim: Dur3 mediates the high-affinity transport of urea.
source: The Dur3 mediates the high-affinity transport of urea.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact about Dur3 function.

claim: The Dur3 mRNA level increased significantly during seed germination.
source: The Dur3 mRNA level increased significantly during seed germination (Bu et al., 2015; van Zelm et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bu et al., 2015; van Zelm et al., 2020.

claim: AtDur3 may be involved in long-distance urea transport from cotyledons to radicles.
source: According to our initial study, blocking the transport of free urea generated by the arginine hydrolysis pathway may also alleviate SISG (Figure 7), and AtDur3 may be involved in long-distance urea transport from cotyledons to radicles.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the atdur3 mutant analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Urea transport and the arginine hydrolysis pathway may synergistically affect SISG.
source: Urea transport and the arginine hydrolysis pathway may synergistically affect SISG.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined effects of urea transport and arginine hydrolysis on SISG.

claim: The application of PPD treatment across a diverse range of plants demonstrated consistent underlying principles.
source: Although our evidence is primarily derived from studies on Arabidopsis, the application of PPD treatment across a diverse range of plants, including glycophytes, halophytes, graminaceous crops, and legumes, demonstrated consistent underlying principles.
